text.p: A three-judge federal court panel adjourned with no ruling on Tuesday after hearing Norfolk Southern Corp's appeal of a lower-court ruling that refused to block provisions that protect the proposed merger between Conrail Inc and CSX Corp.

Norfolk Southern's attorney, Steven Rothschild, said that by granting CSX options on millions of shares, and by allowing CSX to vote its 19.9 percent of Conrail's stock, Conrail is "impermissibly delegating" and "inappropriately abdicating" the responsibility of its current board to a third party -- CSX Corp -- by the conveyance of authority those shares carry.

In addition, the exclusivity provision in the current deal between Conrail and CSX, which prohibits Conrail from seeking or accepting any other mergers until 1999, is "coercive" to Conrail's stockholders and allows Conrail and CSX to continue to tinker with their pact until they succeed, Rothschild argued.

The longer CSX and Conrail have, the greater the chances for a vote by Conrail shareholders to exempt Conrail from a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail, Rothschild said.

In a session that lasted just over an hour, the judges heard arguments from attorneys representing all three railroad giants, as well as from an attorney trying a class-action suit brought by some Conrail shareholders who allege that Conrail's recommendation of CSX's tender offer inadequately disclosed the full value of Conrail's stock.
Norfolk's appeal and the class-action suit were consolidated by the Third Circuit Court of Appeals here.
Norfolk Southern has started a hostile takeover of Conrail by offering $115 per share in cash for all of Conrail's stock, a deal valued at about $10.3 billion.

CSX has offered $110 per share in cash for up to 40 percent of Conrail's stock, and has offered CSX stock for the remaining 60 percent, in a deal valued at about $1 billion less than Norfolk Southern's offer.
"What they (Conrail and CSX) do is get as many free shots as they want," Rothschild said in contesting the exclusivity provision.
Rothschild refers to the provision as a "lock-out" provision, while the judges and the attorneys for Conrail and CSX refer to it as a "no-shop" provision.

"Irreparable harm has been caused by allowing CSX to vote their shares. What the Conrail shareholders are being deprived of (through the exclusivity provision) is the right to have the directors of Conrail act on anything that comes across the transome (until the merger with CSX is either completed or fails). Their directors are incorrectly foreclosed from carrying out their fiduciary duties," Rothschild said.

Theodore Mirvis, arguing on behalf of CSX, said the exclusivity period does not present irreparable harm to the legal rights of Norfolk Southern, and that Pennsylvania's distinct merger laws allow Conrail's board to impose such a restriction.
"To say that that conduct, which is permitted and very specially protected, is then subject to (court) review...is clearly contradictory to the Pennsylvania Legislature," Mirvis said.

Board decisions "cannot be found to be in breach of fiduciary duties because of their effect on tender offers or merger offers. We think it is inherent (in the Pennsylvania statutes) that directors act as gatekeepers. There is no indication whatsoever that the no-shop provision is causing irreparable consequences," Mirvis said.
Conrail's attorney, Thomas Van Kirk, said Conrail's board took appropriate action to prevent the company from being raided by both Norfolk Southern and CSX.

Van Kirk said negotiations in 1994 between Conrail and Norfolk Southern failed to bring about a stock-swap merger. "It was then in 1995 that Norfolk Southern and CSX got together to decided whether to carve up Conrail," he said.

Conrail, after 1995, "entered into strategic planning negotiations...and what they decided to do is to enter into a strategic merger with CSX. They had the right to do that and were fulfilling their fiduciary duties," Van Kirk said, adding, "To this day, Norfolk Southern has never made a merger proposal to Conrail's board of directors."

Before closing the session, Judge Walter Stapleton told the attorneys he found their arguments well presented, but he expressed some doubts as to the outcome of Norfolk's appeal when he said to Rothschild: "I agree with you that it seems to me clearly that these appeals are not moot. But what could we do that would change the status quo?"
The court is expected to issue a decision in six to eight weeks.
